moments.title: Academie francaise founded
moments.body:
Richelieu gives letters patent on 29 January 1635 to formalise an academy that will regulate the French language.

The Academie has 40 'immortels'.
moments.takeaway: Language policy was instituted as a state project under absolutism.

moments.title: First Dictionnaire de l'Academie
moments.body: The first edition appears after sixty years of work. Successive editions follow into the 20th century; the ninth edition was completed in 2024.
moments.takeaway: Codification of standard French is a multi-century institutional process.

moments.title: Gregoire's report on patois
moments.body: Gregoire reports that fewer than half of French citizens speak standard French. The Revolution begins linking language standardisation to national identity.
moments.takeaway: Revolutionary politics turned linguistic uniformity into a republican project.

now.title: French today
now.body: OIF estimates around 320 million French speakers worldwide, with sharply rising figures projected for francophone Africa. Loi Toubon (1994) regulates language in commercial and official contexts.
now.open_questions: How will French evolve as its demographic centre shifts? How will the Academie respond to inclusive writing and other reforms?

items.reflection: French illustrates how strongly state institutions can shape the trajectory of a language over centuries.

moments.title: L'Etre et le Neant
moments.body: Sartre's existentialist treatise appears under Occupation. Phenomenology meets the wartime question of choice under constraint.
moments.takeaway: Foundational French philosophy of the 20th century was written under extreme political conditions.

moments.title: Le Deuxieme Sexe
moments.body: Beauvoir's two-volume study introduces the line 'On ne nait pas femme: on le devient', shaping later feminist theory.
moments.takeaway: The 20th century's leading French intellectuals worked across philosophy, fiction and politics.

moments.title: Camus wins the Nobel
moments.body: Camus, the second-youngest Nobel literature laureate at the time, dies in a car accident in 1960.
moments.takeaway: International recognition placed French literature at the centre of post-war cultural debate.

now.title: French letters today
now.body: Contemporary writing includes prizewinning authors with diverse backgrounds (Modiano, Erpenbeck, NDiaye, Bouraoui). Translation flows have shifted with global publishing.
now.open_questions: How are postcolonial francophone literatures reshaping the French canon?

items.reflection: Major French intellectual movements have repeatedly emerged in dialogue with political crisis.

moments.title: Parlez-vous franglais?
moments.body:
Etiemble's polemic against anglicisms popularises 'franglais' as a term of criticism.

Debate over English borrowing intensifies.
moments.takeaway: Language anxieties have recurred in similar forms across the 20th century.

moments.title: Loi Toubon
moments.body:
French law mandates French in commercial advertising, employment contracts and public-sector communication.

The Constitutional Council narrows some provisions on freedom-of-expression grounds.
moments.takeaway: Language regulation works alongside, not in place of, constitutional rights.

moments.title: Academie endorses 'courriel'
moments.body:
Following Quebec's lead, the Academie recommends 'courriel' for email.

Later recommendations include 'mot-diese' for hashtag and 'jeu video en nuage' for cloud gaming.
moments.takeaway: Official terminology and everyday usage often diverge in practice.

now.title: Linguistic policy today
now.body: Inclusive writing debates, regional language rights and digital terminology continue. Le Robert and Larousse track usage rather than prescribe it.
now.open_questions: How will France balance the Academie's recommendations against international French usage?

items.reflection: Cycles of borrowing and resistance are themselves part of French linguistic history.

moments.title: Onesime Reclus coins 'francophonie'
moments.body: The geographer Reclus introduces the term to describe the community of French speakers worldwide.
moments.takeaway: The concept of a francophone community predates institutional structures.

moments.title: ACCT founded
moments.body: The Agence de cooperation culturelle et technique (later OIF) is founded as the institutional core of la Francophonie.
moments.takeaway: International francophone institutions emerged with decolonisation.

moments.title: African demographic centre
moments.body:
Projections suggest the majority of French speakers will live in Africa by 2050.

DR Congo and other states with French as official or working language drive the shift.
moments.takeaway: The geography of major world languages is being reshaped by African demography.

now.title: Francophonie today
now.body: OIF includes 88 states and governments. Many use French as a second language alongside others; education systems remain central to its spread.
now.open_questions: How does African francophone literature and media reshape the language? What role will French play alongside English and Mandarin globally?

items.reflection: The future of a language often depends on demographic trends well outside the country whose name it bears.

moments.title: Caesar's Gallic Wars
moments.body: Roman conquest of Gaul brings Latin to the territory now called France. Gaulish slowly retreats.
moments.takeaway: France's language has Roman occupation at its root.

moments.title: Strasbourg Oaths
moments.who: Louis the German and Charles the Bald
moments.body: The earliest substantial text in Old French (with Old High German version) is sworn between Charlemagne's grandsons.
moments.takeaway: Political alliances generated some of the earliest written French.

moments.title: Ordinance of Villers-Cotterets
moments.body: Francis I orders French (not Latin) be used in legal documents across the realm.
moments.takeaway: Royal power shaped which language became standard.

now.title: Old French today
now.body: Old French is taught in universities; medievalists keep updating editions of Chretien de Troyes and the chansons de geste.
now.open_questions: How do we hear a language nobody speaks any more?

items.reflection: French's deepest history is half Latin and half political.

moments.title: Tartuffe
moments.body: Moliere's satire on religious hypocrisy is banned for five years after Catholic protest.
moments.takeaway: Comedy was politically dangerous under Louis XIV.

moments.title: Andromaque
moments.body: Racine's tragedy, in classical alexandrines, defines French neoclassical drama.
moments.takeaway: French classical theatre built strict formal conventions.

moments.title: Moliere dies on stage
moments.body: Moliere collapses during a performance of Le Malade imaginaire and dies hours later.
moments.takeaway: Some artists die in the act of performance.

now.title: Classical theatre now
now.body: Comedie-Francaise continues Moliere's company. Racine and Moliere remain core school texts in France.
now.open_questions: How do alexandrines translate for contemporary audiences?

items.reflection: French theatre invented its own classicism in the 17th century.

moments.title: Encyclopedie published
moments.body: The 28-volume Encyclopedie organises human knowledge with Enlightenment values.
moments.takeaway: Reference works were ideological projects.

moments.title: Candide
moments.body: Voltaire's satire savages Leibnizian optimism after the Lisbon earthquake.
moments.takeaway: Philosophical fiction shaped public opinion.

moments.title: Du contrat social
moments.body: Rousseau's 'The Social Contract' opens 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'

quote.text: L'homme est ne libre, et partout il est dans les fers.

moments.takeaway: Enlightenment thought set up the conceptual ground for the Revolution.

now.title: Enlightenment now
now.body: Voltaire and Rousseau remain on the bac syllabus. Their political vocabulary still shapes republican discourse.
now.open_questions: Which Enlightenment values most need reaffirming today?

items.reflection: France's 18th-century writers gave the Revolution its words before it found its weapons.

moments.title: Storming of the Bastille
moments.body: On 14 July 1789 a Paris crowd takes the Bastille fortress. The date becomes France's national day.
moments.takeaway: Symbolic acts can outlast their tactical purpose.

moments.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man
moments.body: The Declaration enshrines liberty, equality and resistance to oppression.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional language shaped global human rights vocabulary.

moments.title: Execution of Louis XVI
moments.body: The king is guillotined on 21 January 1793, followed by Marie Antoinette in October.
moments.takeaway: The Revolution moved from reform to regicide in four years.

now.title: Revolution's legacy
now.body: Liberte, egalite, fraternite remains the Republic's motto. Bastille Day parades march down the Champs-Elysees.
now.open_questions: How are revolutionary ideals still contested in contemporary France?

items.reflection: Modern French political identity is dated from a summer of crowds.

moments.title: 18 Brumaire coup
moments.body: Napoleon's coup ends the Directory and begins the Consulate.
moments.takeaway: Revolution and authoritarianism repeatedly cycled.

moments.title: Code civil
moments.body: The Napoleonic Code influences legal systems in much of Europe, Latin America and beyond.
moments.takeaway: Legal codes can outlast empires.

moments.title: Waterloo
moments.body: Napoleon's defeat ends his 100 days. He is exiled to Saint Helena.
moments.takeaway: European geopolitics was reset by one battle.

now.title: Napoleon's legacy now
now.body: The Code civil still underpins French law. Napoleon's status as hero or tyrant remains contested.
now.open_questions: How should France remember an emperor who reinstated slavery in 1802?

items.reflection: Modern French institutions are still organised by Napoleon's choices.

moments.title: Hernani battle
moments.body: Romantic supporters of Hugo's play clash with classicists at the premiere of Hernani.
moments.takeaway: Theatrical battles registered cultural change.

moments.title: La Comedie humaine
moments.body: Balzac plans a series of 137 interconnected novels to map French society.
moments.takeaway: 19th-century novelists thought encyclopedically.

moments.title: Les Miserables
moments.body: Hugo's 1,500-page novel is published almost simultaneously in multiple countries.
moments.takeaway: Mass literacy made international literary events possible.

now.title: 19th-century classics now
now.body: Les Miserables is now a global musical and film. Balzac's novels remain in print.
now.open_questions: What do these long novels offer in an age of short attention?

items.reflection: France's 19th century created the realist novel as we know it.

moments.title: Madame Bovary trial
moments.body: Flaubert is tried for offending morality. The same year, Baudelaire's Les Fleurs du Mal is censored.
moments.takeaway: Literary modernity arrived through court cases.

moments.title: Naturalist manifesto
moments.body: Zola's 'Le roman experimental' lays out naturalism as a scientific approach to fiction.
moments.takeaway: Literary movements wrote their own theory.

moments.title: J'accuse...!
moments.body: Zola's open letter denouncing antisemitism in the Dreyfus Affair reshapes the role of the public intellectual.
moments.takeaway: Literature met front-page politics.

now.title: 19th-century realism now
now.body: Flaubert's prose remains a stylistic benchmark. Zola's documentary methods anticipated contemporary investigative writing.
now.open_questions: Which contemporary writers are this generation's Zolas?

items.reflection: French realism made novels into social science.

moments.title: July Revolution
moments.body: Three days of fighting (les Trois Glorieuses) topple Charles X. Louis-Philippe becomes 'citizen king'.
moments.takeaway: France entered repeated cycles of revolution after 1789.

moments.title: Second Republic
moments.body: The February Revolution ends the July Monarchy. Universal male suffrage is introduced (women excluded).
moments.takeaway: Revolutionary moments produce uneven progress.

moments.title: Paris Commune
moments.body: After France's defeat by Prussia, Paris workers establish a self-governing commune for 72 days, ending in 'Bloody Week' (Semaine Sanglante).
moments.takeaway: Revolutionary moments can be brief and devastating.

now.title: Republican memory
now.body: The Communards' Wall in Pere Lachaise remains a pilgrimage site. May Day strikes invoke Commune history.
now.open_questions: How does France remember internal violence?

items.reflection: France has had five Republics, two Empires and several Monarchies since 1789.

moments.title: Dreyfus convicted
moments.body: Captain Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish artillery officer, is wrongly convicted of treason and sent to Devil's Island.
moments.takeaway: Judicial process can be deeply contaminated by prejudice.

moments.title: J'accuse...!
moments.body: Zola's open letter denouncing the army's role in Dreyfus's conviction triggers national crisis.
moments.takeaway: The Dreyfus Affair polarised France into pro- and anti-Dreyfusards.

moments.title: Dreyfus exonerated
moments.body: Dreyfus is fully exonerated and reinstated. He serves in World War I.
moments.takeaway: Restorative justice can take a generation.

now.title: Dreyfus's legacy
now.body: The Affair shaped French press, Republican identity and Zionism (Herzl was a reporter at the trial). Recent biopics renew public memory.
now.open_questions: How does the Affair speak to contemporary antisemitism?

items.reflection: A single miscarriage of justice can split a nation for a decade.

moments.title: France enters WWI
moments.body: France mobilises against Germany. Trench warfare follows along the Western Front.
moments.takeaway: World War I left scars across French villages.

moments.title: Battle of Verdun
moments.body: Verdun lasts ten months with over 700,000 casualties.
moments.takeaway: Verdun became a French national symbol of endurance.

moments.title: Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
moments.body: An unknown soldier is interred under the Arc de Triomphe; an eternal flame is lit in 1923.
moments.takeaway: WWI created new rituals of national mourning.

now.title: WWI memory today
now.body: Centenary commemorations (2014-2018) renewed interest. Trench archaeology continues in northern France.
now.open_questions: How will WWI be remembered as the last survivors' children pass?

items.reflection: France's countryside still preserves WWI's geography.

moments.title: Fall of France
moments.body: France falls in six weeks. Marshal Petain signs the armistice; Vichy regime collaborates with Germany.
moments.takeaway: France's WWII trauma began with rapid defeat.

moments.title: De Gaulle's London appeal
moments.body: De Gaulle calls for resistance from London on 18 June 1940.
moments.takeaway: The Free French were a media phenomenon as well as a military force.

moments.title: Liberation of Paris
moments.body: Paris is liberated on 25 August 1944. De Gaulle marches down the Champs-Elysees.
moments.takeaway: Liberation became national myth.

now.title: WWII memory
now.body: France acknowledged state responsibility for Vichy deportations in 1995 (Chirac). Holocaust memorial sites are increasingly visited.
now.open_questions: How does France hold both Resistance heroism and collaboration in memory?

items.reflection: France's 20th century is unimaginable without the Resistance myth and its complications.

moments.title: Algerian War
moments.body: The war kills hundreds of thousands and ends in Algerian independence.
moments.takeaway: Decolonisation reshaped French politics.

moments.title: Fifth Republic established
moments.body: De Gaulle returns to power amid Algerian crisis; a new constitution gives the presidency stronger powers.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional change followed colonial crisis.

moments.title: May 1968 protests
moments.body: Student protests and a general strike paralyse France for weeks. De Gaulle resigns the next year.
moments.takeaway: Cultural and labour unrest can topple governments.

now.title: Fifth Republic now
now.body: Macron's second term faces continuing protest cultures. The presidency remains powerful.
now.open_questions: What replaces de Gaulle's institutional settlement?

items.reflection: France's current institutions were shaped in a colonial emergency.

moments.title: Lumiere brothers' first films
moments.body: France launches commercial cinema with the first paying public screenings.
moments.takeaway: Cinema is one of France's earliest gifts to global culture.

moments.title: Les Quatre Cents Coups
moments.body: Truffaut's autobiographical film, made for $75,000, helps launch the Nouvelle Vague.
moments.takeaway: A generation of critics became directors.

moments.title: A bout de souffle
moments.body: Godard's jump-cut, hand-held style and direct-address performance reshape film language.
moments.takeaway: Cinema technique can change in months.

now.title: French cinema today
now.body: Cesar Awards, Cannes and a state-funded production system sustain French film. Streaming pressures and culture quotas continue.
now.open_questions: How does French cinema compete with global streaming?

items.reflection: France invented cinema and then reinvented it in a Paris cafe.

moments.title: Nuit des barricades
moments.body: On 10 May, students build barricades in the Latin Quarter; police clear them in violent overnight confrontations.
moments.takeaway: Cobblestones and graffiti became symbols of an era.

moments.title: 10 million on strike
moments.body: By late May, an estimated 10 million workers strike across France.
moments.takeaway: Cultural revolt connected to industrial action.

moments.title: De Gaulle resigns
moments.body: De Gaulle resigns after losing a referendum. The post-war political settlement is over.
moments.takeaway: Protest can end careers.

now.title: Protest culture today
now.body: Gilets jaunes (2018-19), pension protests (2023) and Charlie Hebdo solidarity all draw on May 68 imagery.
now.open_questions: How do contemporary protests use 1968 vocabulary?

items.reflection: France's modern political imagination still passes through May 68.

moments.title: Treaty of Rome
moments.body: France is a founding member of the European Economic Community.
moments.takeaway: France helped invent the EU.

moments.title: Schengen Agreement
moments.body: France signs Schengen near the Luxembourg border. Passport-free travel follows in 1995.
moments.takeaway: Borders within Europe became more porous.

moments.title: Euro launched
moments.body: The franc gives way to the euro for currency in 1999 and notes/coins in 2002.
moments.takeaway: France gave up monetary sovereignty for European integration.

now.title: EU and France now
now.body: France remains a central EU player. Macron promotes 'European sovereignty'. Far-right Euroscepticism rises.
now.open_questions: What does French leadership of the EU look like next?

items.reflection: France's borders feel different than they did 50 years ago.

moments.title: Banlieue riots
moments.body: After two teenagers die fleeing police in Clichy-sous-Bois, three weeks of unrest spread across France.
moments.takeaway: Urban marginalisation produced political crisis.

moments.title: Charlie Hebdo and Bataclan attacks
moments.body: January's attack on Charlie Hebdo's offices and November's coordinated attacks on Paris venues kill 147.
moments.takeaway: France faced sustained terrorist violence in 2015.

moments.title: Gilets jaunes
moments.body: Yellow-vest protests against fuel taxes, government policy and inequality continue for months.
moments.takeaway: Tax changes can ignite class grievances.

now.title: France today
now.body: Macron faces RN opposition, pension protests and ongoing debates about secularism. The 2024 Olympics presented France to the world.
now.open_questions: How does France balance republican unity with diversity?

items.reflection: France's 21st century has involved repeated reckonings with its own diversity and inequality.

moments.title: Law on separation of Church and State
moments.body: The 1905 law establishes laicite, removing public funding for religion.
moments.takeaway: French secularism is a specific historical settlement.

moments.title: Headscarf law
moments.body: Conspicuous religious symbols, including the Islamic headscarf, are banned in state schools.
moments.takeaway: Laicite's interpretation has evolved with immigration.

moments.title: Burqa ban
moments.body: Full face coverings are banned in public space. The law is upheld by the European Court of Human Rights.
moments.takeaway: Religious dress became a battleground for republican identity.

now.title: Laicite today
now.body: Debates continue over the abaya in schools, public swimming and Catholic processions. Macron's 'separatism' law (2021) intensified controversy.
now.open_questions: How can laicite be both neutral and applied unevenly?

items.reflection: France's secularism is at once principle and battleground.

moments.title: Quebec City founded
moments.body: Champlain establishes a permanent French settlement on the St Lawrence.
moments.takeaway: France's North American empire began with a fort.

moments.title: Treaty of Paris
moments.body: France cedes most of New France to Britain after the Seven Years' War.
moments.takeaway: Quebec became British politically but remained French culturally.

moments.title: Quebec independence referendum
moments.body: The independence side loses by less than 1%. The Bill 96 language law (2022) strengthens French in Quebec.
moments.takeaway: Linguistic nationhood remains contested.

now.title: Quebec today
now.body: Quebec maintains French through Bill 101 and successors. Montreal remains a major francophone city.
now.open_questions: What does the future of Quebec French look like?

items.reflection: Some of the strongest French communities have lived outside France for generations.

moments.title: Year of African independence
moments.body: Fourteen francophone African states gain independence in a single year.
moments.takeaway: Decolonisation came in waves.

moments.title: Senghor's Negritude
moments.body: Senghor, the first president of Senegal, articulates negritude as a francophone literary movement.
moments.takeaway: African intellectuals reshaped what French meant.

moments.title: CFA franc reforms
moments.body: The eco currency replaces the West African CFA franc, ending decades of French monetary tutelage.
moments.takeaway: Postcolonial relationships continue to be renegotiated.

now.title: Francafrique today
now.body: France's military presence in the Sahel has contracted. Coups in Mali, Niger and Burkina Faso challenge French influence.
now.open_questions: How does Francafrique evolve in the multipolar world?

items.reflection: France's African footprint is changing fast.

moments.title: L'Etranger
moments.body: Camus's novel of an Algerian-born French clerk who kills an Arab on a beach defines the literature of the absurd.
moments.takeaway: Camus's work emerged from his Algerian roots.

moments.title: La Peste
moments.body: Camus's plague novel becomes an allegory for occupation and resistance.
moments.takeaway: Fiction can hold political and metaphysical questions together.

moments.title: Camus dies in car crash
moments.body: Camus dies aged 46 with an unused train ticket in his pocket.
moments.takeaway: Some biographies become inseparable from the work.

now.title: Camus today
now.body: La Peste returned to bestseller lists in 2020 during COVID. Postcolonial readings (Kamel Daoud's Meursault, contre-enquete, 2013) continue.
now.open_questions: How do we read Camus alongside Algerian voices?

items.reflection: A pied-noir who never quite settled in either France or Algeria gave the language a new register.

moments.title: Loi Deixonne
moments.body: After decades of repression, regional languages (Breton, Basque, Catalan, Occitan) are allowed to be taught in schools.
moments.takeaway: France's diversity was long denied institutionally.

moments.title: Constitution amendment
moments.body: Article 2 declares French 'the language of the Republic', complicating regional language protection.
moments.takeaway: Constitutional language reinforced monolingual policy.

moments.title: Regional languages constitutional
moments.body: Article 75-1 recognises regional languages as part of France's heritage.
moments.takeaway: Recognition does not necessarily mean support.

now.title: Regional languages today
now.body: Bilingual schools (Diwan in Brittany, calandretes in Occitania) operate with mixed legal status. The Falloux law on minority-language teachers continues to provoke debate.
now.open_questions: Will France's minority languages survive as living tongues?

items.reflection: France's linguistic uniformity was achieved at the cost of many other tongues.
